solver.kind: blind AI solver B (separate agent, answer-free packet, adversarial rubric)

E067-01.notes: Singular possessive of 'country' (one nation). 'countrys'' is not a word; B lacks possession; D is plural possessive, but there is only one country.

E067-02.notes: The 1880 tally is a completed past event, so simple past 'needed' fits. Present perfect clashes with the past setting; 'will need' is wrong; 'needing' leaves the clause after the colon without a main verb.

E067-03.notes: The ticket-punching anecdote links to sentence 5's hole-punched cards. A misreads the anecdote's focus; B is false, since the sentence does not explain the delay; C is false, since there is no contradiction. Fact check: the conductor 'punch photograph' story is Hollerith's own account, and 'according to one account' hedges it properly.

E067-04.notes: Participial phrase modifying the action. 'completes' is a tense shift and makes the sentence ungrammatical; 'and completing' is not parallel with 'passed...and touched'; 'it completed' creates a comma splice. Fact check: pins dropping through holes into mercury cups, closing circuits that advance dials, is accurate.

flags.note: 'their' can be read as singular they referring to 'a clerk' (the clerk's reading of the dials). Many current style guides accept that use, so a test-wise reader could defend NO CHANGE. The intended antecedent is 'Each dial' (singular, so 'its'), but 'a clerk' sits closer to the pronoun than 'Each dial' does. Suggest rewording to remove the clerk reading, e.g. '...at the end of the day a clerk recorded the number [its] needle showed' or 'a clerk wrote down [its] final count', or name the dial again.

E067-05.notes: Key is 'its' (the dial's reading). 'it's' and 'they're' are contractions and fail.

E067-06.notes: Sentence 10 gives an example of the 'dramatic' results. Nevertheless, Instead, and Otherwise each signal a contrast or alternative that is not there. Fact check: the 1890 population total was announced about six weeks into processing, so 'within weeks' is accurate.

E067-07.notes: No colon after 'such as'. A semicolon cannot set off a nonclause phrase. The comma before nonrestrictive 'such as' in C is acceptable. Dropping the comma is not offered without a colon, so there is no competing answer. Fact check: railroad freight (e.g., New York Central) and business accounting uses are accurate.

E067-08.notes: Redundancy item; A, C and D repeat themselves. B is concise and still accurate. Fact check: the Tabulating Machine Company was founded in 1896, merged into CTR in 1911, and was renamed IBM in 1924, so 'after a merger, eventually...became' is accurate.

E067-09.notes: Only D returns to the first paragraph's problem of counting a growing nation. A, B and C are relevant facts that do not make that connection. Fact check: punched cards were widely used into the 1970s, true. Hollerith died in Washington, D.C., in November 1929 after retiring around 1921, so 'several years' is fine. IBM built early commercial computers (701/650), true. The echo of 'growing nation' is a legitimate textual link, not a giveaway.

E067-10.notes: The essay runs problem, then invention, then mechanism, then impact. B overstates the IBM material. C is false. D is false, because paragraph 2 explains the mechanism. Fact check: the 1880 census taking nearly eight years is the standard claim (final reports ran to 1888); Hollerith worked on the 1880 census, true; 'young engineer' is fine.

E067-11.notes: A, C and D are redundant, and D is doubly so. Fact check on the Halifax essay: Dec. 6, 1917, Mont-Blanc/Imo collision, burning ship drifting toward Pier 6, about 9:04 explosion, about 2,000 deaths, Vince Coleman's telegraph warning, Boston relief train and the Dec. 7 blizzard, tree sent in 1918 and every year since 1971. All accurate. Other errors in the passage (sentence 2 comma, sentence 3 'they', sentence 9 agreement, 'in spite', sentence 15 comma splice) are presumably targets of other items.
